summary:
Quebec stands under the national framework of Canada, where gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply in Quebec as they do in every other province.

Provincial law adds a second layer. Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has listed gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination since 2016, and the enforcement machinery produces findings. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on the ground of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

The scope of Quebec's own statute has been litigated to judgment. After a two-month trial heard with 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court held in 2021 QCCS 191 that provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec were invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision in 2024 QCCA 348, and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. Visitors carrying Quebec-issued identity documents therefore deal with a statutory scheme that has been rebuilt around recognition rather than medical gatekeeping.

Correctional placement runs against the national direction. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, describing fairness and safety as the priorities. The directive was issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison, and advocates state that the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This reverses the previous provincial practice of weighing gender identity in placement, and it bears on a trans visitor only if that visitor is detained.

National hate-crime data gives no Quebec-specific figure. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000; that rate fell 2% in 2024 but stands 142% above 2018. Provincial rates ranged from 5.3 per 100,000 in Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador to 16.0 in Ontario, with eight provinces stable or declining. The release carries no Quebec rate.
tangentialFactors:
The hate-crime figures above rest on an underlying analysis by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation that examines national police-reported data including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations. Its framing is advocacy-adjacent, and its motive categories are narrower than the totals published by Statistics Canada.

The correctional directive arrives amid wider Canadian debate over where transgender prisoners are held. Federal policy since Bill C-16 is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; a 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. Quebec's 2025 directive cuts against that federal posture rather than with it.

The national picture on recorded hate crime is drifting downward for sexual-minority motivation at the same time as the long-run rate is rising sharply: incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658 in 2024 from a 2023 peak of 889, ending three consecutive years of increases, within an overall series up 142% since 2018.
localsOnly:
Trans people make up a small share of Quebec's residents: 2021 census data cited by Éducaloi records that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older identify as transgender, rising to 0.27% among those aged 15 to 34.

Discrimination complaints under the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms are available to residents as well as visitors, and the tribunal's 2024 award of moral and punitive damages shows the remedy is monetary and enforceable rather than declaratory only.

The reform of the Civil Code following the Centre for Gender Advocacy litigation governs how Quebec residents amend the sex designation on provincial civil-status documents, so birth certificates and Quebec identity cards issued after the reform follow the new rules rather than the pre-2024 ones.

The June 2025 placement directive governs where Quebec incarcerates transgender people held in the provincial system, and it applies to residents of the province first.
outOfScopeNotes:
Statistics Canada's 30 March 2026 release gives no Quebec-specific hate-crime rate or count in the available windows, so the province's position relative to the 5.3 to 16.0 provincial range is unresolved on this inventory rather than established.

Whether the Egale Canada analysis breaks out gender-identity-motivated incidents separately from sexual-orientation incidents for Quebec is not sourced here; only the existence of those motive categories in its national analysis is.

No source in this inventory establishes a Quebec rule on restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities beyond the national statement that no jurisdiction restricts trans use of them, and none addresses visitor screening, visa or border practice for Quebec specifically.

The claim that advocates regard the June 2025 correctional directive as a violation of the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms is reported; no court ruling on the directive itself appears in this inventory, so its legal status is unresolved.

Whether Quebec's post-litigation Civil Code provisions match the federal X marker regime on travel documents is not addressed by the sources assembled here.
